opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that pre-training gives you a prior over behaviors, and RL is mostly a process of reweighting that prior rather than discovering things from scratch. Early in RL, the model is not learning new skills so much as figuring out which of the many things it already half-knows how to do actually get rewarded.

Concretely, RL only works if you get some signal. If the model never stumbles onto a correct answer, the gradient is basically zero and you learn nothing. Pre-training is what puts you in the regime where, out of a bunch of samples, a few succeed. Once you have even a small success rate, RL can amplify it very quickly. That's why the early curves often look so steep: you're taking behaviors that were present with low probability, say a careful chain of reasoning or checking your own work, and making them the default.

There's an interesting implication there. A lot of what looks like the model "learning to reason" in early RL is closer to elicitation. The circuits were mostly built during pre-training, from all the humans online explaining their thinking, debugging code, writing proofs. RL is selecting for those modes and suppressing the sloppy, shortcut-y ones. You see this in how sample-efficient early RL is relative to how much it seems to change the model's behavior. Small amounts of compute can produce big qualitative shifts.

The open question, and I think it's genuinely contested, is how far that goes. Is RL forever bounded by what's latent in pre-training, or, with enough compute and long enough horizons, does it start building genuinely new capabilities? My intuition is that the early phase is mostly reweighting, but as you scale RL and the model chains together behaviors in novel ways over long tasks, you get compositional novelty that's real, even if every individual piece came from pre-training. A stronger base model raises the floor, and it also raises how far RL can take you, because there's more to compose. So pre-training and RL aren't substitutes. They're deeply complementary, and the quality of the prior largely sets the pace of everything that comes after.

r001.rationale: The response says that without occasionally producing a correct answer, the model gets no useful gradient or learning signal.

r002.rationale: It explains that pre-training makes some sampled attempts succeed, allowing RL to amplify those behaviors instead of beginning with no signal.

r003.rationale: It describes early RL as eliciting capabilities built during pre-training, but does not connect that effect to learning from one example.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that pre-training is giving you the prior over which RL does its search. When you do RL on a language model, you're not learning from scratch the way you would in, say, Atari or Go, where the policy starts out as basically random and every bit of signal has to come from the reward. Here the model already has an incredibly rich distribution over behaviors, and what RL is doing in those early steps is mostly reweighting things the model can already do rather than teaching it genuinely new capabilities.

That has a few consequences that I think are underappreciated. The first is that the early learning dynamics are almost entirely about exploration being cheap. If the base model puts, say, one percent probability on the right chain of reasoning for a math problem, then with a handful of samples you'll hit it, you'll get a positive reward, and you can sharpen on it. If the base model puts effectively zero probability on it, RL just doesn't get off the ground, no matter how good your algorithm is. So the quality of pre-training determines what's reachable at all, and a lot of what looks like "RL working" is really "pre-training made the right behaviors sampleable."

The second thing is that pre-training shapes the representations in a way that makes credit assignment much easier than it should be. The model already has notions of what a correct step looks like, what a checked answer looks like, when it's confused. So when you give it a sparse end-of-episode reward, the gradient doesn't have to invent those concepts, it just has to connect them to the reward. That's why you see these very fast early gains, where a relatively small amount of RL compute produces a big jump. You're mostly just turning the dial on latent behaviors the model already has.

And then the third piece, which is the one I find most interesting, is where that regime ends. Early on you're exploiting the prior. At some point you've extracted most of what the prior gives you for free, and further progress actually requires the model to discover things that weren't well-represented in pre-training. That transition is where the real questions are, around how much the model can keep learning, whether you need to broaden the pre-training distribution to keep the search tractable, and how much the two stages should be thought of as one continuous process rather than a hand-off. My intuition is that the line between them is going to blur a lot, and that the right frame is that pre-training is really just the part of training where you're buying a very good initialization for whatever comes next.

r001.rationale: The response says the model must sample a successful behavior to receive positive reward, and that if the behavior has effectively zero probability, RL cannot get started.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pretrained models with random-start policies and says early RL can quickly sharpen behaviors the model can already produce, avoiding learning from scratch.

r003.rationale: It explains that apparent RL gains can come from reweighting or eliciting latent behaviors already available from pre-training, rather than creating new capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think pre-training gives you an enormously strong prior over what to try. When you start reinforcement learning, you’re not starting with a system taking random actions. You’re starting with a system that already knows a lot about language, code, and what plausible solutions look like.

So early on, a lot of the improvement can come from changing which of those behaviors the model uses. Suppose it can already solve a problem occasionally, but usually takes a less productive approach. Reinforcement learning can make the successful approach much more likely. That can look like very rapid learning, even though much of the machinery needed to solve the problem was built during pre-training.

But I wouldn’t take that to mean reinforcement learning can only select things the model already knows. That’s a useful picture of the early dynamics. Once you’ve shifted the distribution of attempts, the model starts reaching places where it can get feedback that it rarely encountered before. Then the question becomes how far that process can take you beyond the initial behaviors.

r001.rationale: The response says the model may already solve a problem occasionally and RL can make that approach more likely, but it does not state that occasional success is required to obtain a reward signal for learning.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training gives the model strong prior capabilities, so RL starts with plausible behaviors and can produce rapid early learning because the model can already solve some problems occasionally.

r003.rationale: The response says much of the machinery for solving a problem was built during pre-training, but it does not explain how apparent learning from one example can reflect eliciting a pre-existing capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pre-training makes the early stages of RL look quite different from learning from scratch. You’re starting with a model that already has a huge repertoire of behaviors. It can reason through a problem, check its work, try a different approach—but it won’t necessarily do those things reliably, or in the right context.

So initially, RL can make a lot of progress by changing which of those behaviors the model puts probability on. If it occasionally produces a good solution, and you can recognize that solution, you can reinforce the sequence that got it there. You don’t have to build the whole capability from nothing.

But I wouldn’t take that to mean RL can only select things the model already knows. That’s a useful picture of the early dynamics, not necessarily a limit on what happens later. Once you change the policy, the model starts visiting different trajectories, and those give you opportunities for further learning. The interesting question is where that transition happens: how much of the initial gain is making existing capabilities more reliable, and how much is developing something new?

r001.rationale: The response says RL can reinforce a sequence when the model occasionally produces a good solution and that solution can be recognized.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training gives the model existing behaviors, allowing RL to make early progress by increasing the probability of good solutions rather than building the capability from scratch.

r003.rationale: The response discusses eliciting or reinforcing capabilities already present from pre-training, but does not explain how apparent learning from one example can reflect eliciting those capabilities.
